summary.heading: Current state
summary.text: The December meeting is about the size of the increase, not whether to raise. Staff base case: +25 bp to 4.00–4.25% on 9 Dec, with a material risk of +50 bp (own estimate, about 70% / 30%); a hold is not a realistic outcome. Fedspeak since 5 Nov is uniformly toward tightening (staff barometer +0.75 for 2026 voters, +0.80 all speakers, d). Governor Waller said on 18 Nov that a 50 bp increase is "probably necessary" unless the Committee clearly signals a January move; Williams, Hammack and Logan argue for steady 25 bp steps. The October minutes (18 Nov) say almost all participants see further increases as likely appropriate, and a couple saw more than 25 bp as worth considering if inflation data were unfavourable. Market pricing on 18 Nov fully prices +25 bp with roughly 5% odds of +50 bp (secondary reports). Data: GDPNow 3.2% vs staff Q4 3.0%; October CPI +0.4% / core +0.3%; PPI final demand +0.3%; staff 2026 core PCE about 3.3% Q4/Q4 (own estimate). October core PCE on 25 Nov is the swing input for 25 vs 50. Staff-style view, not Fed Board staff work and not the FOMC SEP (16 Sep medians).

staff_hint: Staff-style view, not Fed Board staff work and not the FOMC SEP.

staff_view.lead: Risk balance (staff view, 20 Nov): growth near baseline, inflation risks still to the upside. Fed speakers lean toward tightening, with most favouring further 25 bp steps (barometer +0.75 for voters, 18 Nov, d), so the debate is 25 vs 50 bp. FIPI-US (30 Oct) is in the high zone with rising momentum; that is a descriptive reading, not a forecast, and it does not change the December +25 bp base case.
bullets: Growth (balanced near term, own estimate): GDPNow 3.2% vs staff Q4 3.0%, gap narrowed from +0.5 to +0.2 pp (d); the New York Fed 2.94% (6 Nov) is close to baseline. Firm nominal retail sales, falling industrial production and weak permits keep the 2027 downside (energy, real incomes, rate-sensitive demand) in place.
Labour (mixed): payrolls +165k and UR 4.1% (October) with U-6 at 7.9%; claims 200k (week ended 7 Nov, advance) still low; SCE unemployment-probability at a post-2020 high (9 Nov).

Inflation (upside risk, smaller): October core CPI +0.3% and PPI less foods, energy & trade +0.5% led to a core PCE reset to about 3.3% (own estimate). The unsealed November CPI research nowcast (+0.20 / +0.30, d) shows no fade in core. Productivity and ECI still offset.

FIPI-US (30 Oct, d): state high, momentum rising (GAP3, distance from the 3-month average), index +1.584. Fed tone hawkish and rising. A US lead of tone over momentum is not established (effective p ≈ 0.07 after overlap adjustment) (d; not pre-registered; with a multiple-lag correction it would not be significant). This is a descriptive classification, not a statistically significant forecast signal (internal FIPI-Momentum v1.1).

Financial conditions: the 10-year eased 5 bp to 5.10% (13 to 17 Nov), with the real yield −2 bp and the staff breakeven (d) −3 bp; the 2s10s spread 0.27 pp and the 5-year breakeven 2.23% (18 Nov). The ACM term premium rose slightly to 0.75% (17 Nov); the Kim-Wright term premium was 0.99% (13 Nov). The models are not averaged.

Fedspeak (5–18 Nov, staff barometer, d): voter mean +0.75, all-speaker mean +0.80 on a −2 to +2 scale. Only Waller (+2) argues for 50 bp; Musalem (+1.5, non-voter) sees several hikes by spring 2027; Logan, Barr and Hammack (+1) back further 25 bp steps; Williams, Goolsbee and Kashkari (+0.5) lean hike without a pace; Bowman and Jefferson (0) give no near-term direction.
Market pricing (18 Nov, secondary reports of a futures-based gauge): +25 bp in December fully priced, about 5% odds of +50 bp, and roughly 75 bp of total increases over 12 months.
staff_view.policy: December call, re-derived 19 Nov: +25 bp to 4.00–4.25% on 9 Dec is the staff base case (own estimate ~70%), +50 bp the main alternative (~30%), and no change below 5%. Why +25: almost all participants expected further increases in the October minutes; the leadership-adjacent voices (Williams) and the 2026 voters Hammack and Logan argue for steady 25 bp steps; markets already price 25 bp, so it tightens without a surprise; October PPI was softer at the headline than October CPI implied. Counter-argument for +50: Waller says 25 bp is enough only with a clear January signal, and the Chair has avoided forward guidance, which by Waller's logic argues for 50; a couple of participants flagged more than 25 bp if inflation data were unfavourable, and October CPI was firm; markets price only about 5% for 50 bp, so the staff weight is well above the market. Triggers: we move to +50 as the base case if October core PCE (25 Nov) is about 0.35% m/m or more and November payrolls (4 Dec) are firm; a hold needs a core PCE print near 0.2% together with clearly weaker payrolls and market stress. This replaces the 13 Nov wording "hold now, +25 bp in December (about 60%)", which understated the hike odds. The staff path is separate from the 16 Sep SEP. Target range 3.75–4.00% (held 10–2 on 28 Oct; Cook and Hammack preferred +25 bp, minutes V).

charts.caption: Source: staff inflation-nowcast model, already-produced pseudo out-of-sample backtest (report label: current vintage, not real-time). As of 6 Nov 2026, 10:46 Europe/Zurich (report timestamp 2026-11-06T09:46:12Z). Actuals: BLS CPI, current vintage, seasonally adjusted, percent month-on-month. The chart is drawn from the already-produced step file; RMSE, MAE and related figures are taken from the already-produced backtest report (same rounding) and its summary JSON. No new model was estimated. This backtest uses revised history, not a real-time vintage. The model in this backtest is a univariate AR(1) on each component’s month-on-month SA series; in production the food component uses persistence and the energy component a gasoline bridge. The October 2025 CPI publication gap, and the non-adjacent November 2025 month, are skipped (shaded band, September 2025–January 2026). US headline model RMSE in the 2023+ sub-period was 0.209 (n=42), as in the same report. A quasi-real-time evaluation against first-release actuals was also produced on 6 Nov 2026, 10:00 Europe/Zurich: US headline RMSE 0.275, n=138. The backtest ends at September 2026 and does not include the October CPI released on 10 Nov. Quality of error statistics: (d).
charts.note: Units are percentage points, month-on-month, seasonally adjusted. Coverage of 80% uses full-sample error quantiles (informative, not expanding sequential bands), as stated in the backtest report.

Fedspeak barometer: scores are staff judgment (d) on a simple −2 to +2 scale, equal weights, latest remark per speaker, 5–18 Nov. Hammack, Williams and Kashkari are scored from press reports, not transcripts (U). Waller's 18 Nov and Goolsbee's 13 Nov views are from live CNBC interviews as reported by CNBC (video not reviewed by the staff). The 2026 voter list is taken from the October minutes voting record (V). There is no speech-based barometer for the 27–28 Oct FOMC; the direction on the tile compares with the voters' revealed positions at that meeting (hold = 0, dissent for +25 bp = +1, minutes V), which is a different basis (indicative only).

Market pricing: from press reports dated 18 Nov 2026 of a third-party futures-based probability gauge (about 95% for +25 bp and 5% for +50 bp; one other report gives 99.9% for +25 bp). The source page itself was not read. A rival 13 Nov report gave more than 10% for +50 bp. Treat as indicative only.
December call weights (about 70/30/under 5) are staff judgment, re-derived 19 Nov, and replace the 13 Nov weights (60/25/15 for +25 / hold / +50), which overstated the chance of a hold.
The November CPI research nowcast (+0.20 / +0.30 m/m) is an unsealed staff-model reading, rated YELLOW, not validated and not a forecast for trading. It is not the sealed nowcast on the main page.

October PPI, retail sales, industrial production and housing figures are carried from staff notes and desk checks of 13, 17 and 18 Nov against BLS and FRED; they were not re-fetched for this note. Census housing figures are first prints with wide error margins. The +0.33% PPI figure is a staff derivation from the BLS series WPSFD49104 as labelled in the 13 Nov note; the series label was not re-verified for this note.
Staff December call weights (about 60/25/15) are judgment, set 13 Nov, not market pricing and not FOMC guidance. The core PCE baseline of about 3.3% is own estimate, pending October PCE on 25 Nov.
BLS published no October CPI year-on-year change (October 2025 gap). Unrounded CPI 0.350 / 0.296 (d) is carried from the 10 Nov staff draft’s API derivation, not re-fetched on 12 Nov.

Leading-indicator charts on this page are as of 23 Nov 2026, 07:26 Europe/Zurich, redrawn from the leading_indicators tidy pull of the same date (public sources only). They were originally added from the Fed Staff Desk note leading_indicators_2026-11-12.md, after the 07:40 cutoff on 12 Nov. Every chart carries a source credit and a “Shown without endorsement by …” line. The best-lag correlation boxes inside the charts are carried from the 12 Nov analysis and were not recomputed on the 23 Nov data.

Several full-sample leads on the leading-indicator charts are driven by 2020–23. Where the pre-pandemic lead is the economically meaningful one and the full-sample best lag is contemporaneous under the 2020 spike, the chart is shifted by the pre-pandemic lead and says so. The 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread is not shifted, because its linear correlation with quarterly real GDP growth is near zero (d).
The Chicago Fed National Financial Conditions Index (NFCI) and its nonfinancial-leverage subindex are shown as the latest vintage only (FRED vintage 12 Nov 2026). There is no real-time vintage test.

There is no October 2026 year-on-year figure for CPI (headline or core) or for import prices excluding fuels, because October 2025 is missing at source. Those gaps are not imputed and are hatched on the charts. The October 2026 import-price level was not in the 17:24 delivery.

The Richmond survey chart is a staff chart of the published manufacturing and non-manufacturing price series, plus an equal-weight staff construction (d) of prices received in months where both sectors exist. It is not an official index and is not given an official index name.

The 1-year expected inflation series is a Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland model product (DOI: https://doi.org/10.26509/frbc-infexp), shown without endorsement by the Bank, for noncommercial use. This page charts only the published output.
The Atlanta Business Inflation Expectations (BIE) year-ahead unit-cost series is shown without endorsement by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, for noncommercial use.

10-year Treasury composition charts are from the Fed Staff Desk note ust10y_decomposition_charts_2026-11-12.md, redrawn from the 17 Nov 2026, 07:17:21 Europe/Zurich tidy pull. H.15 and NY Fed ACM run through 13 November 2026; Board Kim-Wright through 6 November 2026. 11 November was Veterans Day (Board closed; no H.15). Treasury’s own daily CSVs already show 16 November (nominal 5.12, real 2.92, difference 2.20) — a verified figure from this pull, used here only as a caveat and not shown on the public charts.

The 10-year breakeven on every public composition chart is a staff calculation (d): DGS10 minus DFII10, same H.15 date and vintage. FRED T10YIE is not used. On all 5,971 common H.15 days, 2 January 2003–13 November 2026, the staff breakeven equals DGS10 minus DFII10 (max absolute residual 0 within floating-point rounding). The identity does not hold across mixed close dates.

The staff 10-year breakeven is inflation compensation, not pure expected inflation: it embeds an inflation risk premium and is affected by TIPS liquidity (and related frictions), as the Board’s TIPS-curve file (feds200805) states.

The NY Fed ACM model is re-estimated once a month, which “may result in minor changes to the historical decompositions of Treasury yields” (NY Fed product page). This vintage is the official Excel fetched 17 November 07:17:21 Europe/Zurich, daily through 13 November. The daily posting time is undocumented (U as an SLA; V as today’s last date). Do not present a revised history as if it had been known in real time.

Kim-Wright is weekly (Board: typically Tuesday, through the previous Friday). Last observation 6 November 2026, posted 10 November (Board file Last-Modified unchanged on this pull). The 1-day Kim-Wright panel is flagged STALE: the market 12–13 November window has no new KW data. KW is never extrapolated past 6 November. A KW 1-week or 1-month change is KW’s own window ending 6 November, which is not the same as the H.15 window ending 13 November (1-week: KW −8 bp vs H.15 +31 bp).

Term-premium model dependence: ACM 0.725% (13 November) vs Kim-Wright 0.874% (6 November) are different dates. On the last common date, 6 November, the gap is 0.643% vs 0.874%, or 23.1 bp (d). The two models are shown separately and are never averaged. Kim-Wright’s published term premium includes the convexity premium; ACM, as described in the Board Q&A, is a “pure” (ex-convexity) concept. Levels are not strictly comparable; changes are more nearly so, but that is the Board’s wording, not a claim tested here.

The Split B residual is a fitting / curve-basis residual (d), not a liquidity term. It is DGS10 minus the model’s fitted 10-year. DGS10 is a par CMT; ACM is a model fitted to the GSW curve; Kim-Wright is a fitted zero-coupon yield. The residual therefore mixes model fit, par-versus-zero (and on-the-run / H.15 versus the off-the-run GSW universe), and any compounding-convention difference. Compounding conventions for ACM and Kim-Wright were not stated in the file headers and remain unverified from these sources. Residual history is wide (ACM SD 23.7 bp; KW SD 14.6 bp): a quiet residual on one day is not a structural series.

FIPI-US is an internal staff construction (d), source labelled intern. Only the V12R composite is shown (fixed 2000–2019 baseline, H2); licensed component values are not published. Not validated for an investment decision.

FIPI-US momentum is classified with the v1.1 rule GAP3 (distance to the 3-month average) as rising, bottoming, topping or falling. This is a descriptive classification (d), not a forecast signal. The 2020-01 to 2026-10 holdout test was not statistically significant (internal FIPI-Momentum v1.1, Auditor green, 22 Nov 2026). Inflation used in that study is the current vintage only (no real-time ALFRED vintages).

Before Aug 2015 (EA: Dec 2012) the line is a different basket (L9 / EXK9), spliced without adjustment; the splice decision uses the 2015–2026 (EA: 2012–2026) overlap (ex post). The history is pseudo-real-time, not a real-time record. Join gap +0.216 is close to the 0.25 threshold.

blocks.title: Inflation
blocks.read: Mixed, not a clean easing versus the 6 Nov 3.2% core baseline. The 5-year breakeven is softer (T5YIE 2.18 on 20 Nov, from 2.25 on 10 Nov); the Atlanta Fed BIE year-ahead unit-cost mean rose to 2.51% in the November survey (from 2.30% in October); Richmond survey prices and import prices are firmer; GSCPI is still tight but off its September high; Cleveland is near the baseline.

blocks.title: Labour
blocks.read: Labour indicators are consistent with a still-firm labour market at the 4.1% UR baseline. Initial claims remain low: the 4-week average was 197,750 in the week ended 14 Nov (advance), up slightly from 195,750 for the week ended 7 Nov (revised). Nothing here is a clear softening that would undermine the 6 Nov tightening bias on labour-market grounds.

ust10y_decomposition.as_of_display: H.15 and ACM 19 Nov 2026; Kim-Wright 13 Nov 2026
ust10y_decomposition.read: Over the latest H.15 session (18–19 November) the 10-year fell 3 bp (5.07% to 5.04%): the real yield was unchanged (2.88%) and the staff breakeven (d) fell 3 bp (2.19% to 2.16%). In ACM terms the expected-rate component fell about 2 bp (4.34% to 4.32%) and the term premium rose less than 1 bp (0.69% to 0.70%) (d). Kim-Wright, weekly, shows a term premium of 0.99% on 13 November. Over the week (12–19 November) the 10-year fell 6 bp (5.10% to 5.04%), real +2 bp, staff breakeven −8 bp. Over the month (20 October–19 November) the 10-year fell 8 bp (5.12% to 5.04%), real +11 bp, staff breakeven −19 bp. Term-premium levels differ by model, so Split B depends on the model.

reference.direction: More hawkish: +0.62 vs the same voters' 28 Oct positions (+0.12, votes, d)
reference.note: Reference uses the 28 Oct votes from the minutes (hold = 0, dissent for +25 bp = +1), not speeches; indicative only. All 12 voters at 28 Oct: +0.17.

fedspeak_barometer.source: Staff scoring of public remarks; Federal Reserve Board and Reserve Bank texts, CNBC interviews, press reports (U). Not a Federal Reserve product.

speakers.speaker: Christopher Waller
speakers.stance: Hike: a 50 bp increase in December is "probably necessary"; 25 bp only if the Fed clearly signals a January move. "You might need to, like, shock people."
speakers.quality: V (interview, quotes as reported by CNBC)

speakers.speaker: Alberto Musalem
speakers.stance: Hike: "several interest rate increases before the spring of 2027"; real policy rate should be "solidly between 2% and 2.5%".

speakers.speaker: Lorie Logan
speakers.stance: Hike: "at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases"; "may be possible to move more rapidly this winter".

speakers.speaker: Michael Barr
speakers.stance: Hike: "I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further."

speakers.speaker: Beth Hammack
speakers.venue: Ohio State University event (reiterated 16 Nov in a TV interview)
speakers.stance: Hike, gradual: "more frequent, smaller rises"; larger steps only "if we get behind the curve, and I don't think we're behind the curve today".

speakers.speaker: John Williams
speakers.stance: Hike, gradual: likely to raise again, but no need for "dramatic action".

speakers.speaker: Austan Goolsbee
speakers.stance: Leaning hike: the Fed "has definitely got work to do"; no view on pace.
speakers.quality: V (interview, quotes as reported by CNBC)

speakers.speaker: Neel Kashkari
speakers.stance: Leaning hike: the Fed is "clearly missing on inflation side"; no step size.

speakers.speaker: Michelle Bowman
speakers.stance: Wait: further changes "should wait" for a better understanding; benefits of tightening "carefully weighed against its costs".

speakers.speaker: Philip Jefferson
speakers.stance: No direction: inflation "notably above" target; no rate guidance.
